lines: PRESIDENT:  Can you call your witness, please?
MR BURKE:  Yes, sir.  Could I just deal with one
housekeeping matter before I do?  And it's a very
minor point, but it's one that I don't want to be
taken later.  We got the transcript last night, and it
may well be an error in the transcript, but it's more
likely I misspoke, frankly, given how good the Lloyd
Michaux team are.

yesterday on page 86, line 22 to 23 of the transcript.
I thought I had said we had a right of immediate
termination under clause 26.2.2.  The transcript reads
we had no right.  And if I said no, that was misspoke
on my part.  As I say, it's more likely that
I misspoke rather than the transcript is wrong, but
I make the correction now in case it's asserted that
I made an admission.
Otherwise, that's the only housekeeping matter
I had this morning, sir.
PRESIDENT:  So any housekeeping matter, Mr Wygas?
MR WYGAS:  No, sir.  Nothing from the respondents.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.
Have you managed to upload the new document to the
e-bundle?
MR BURKE:  We have.  My understanding is it is at
bundle C, bundle reference {C28}.
PRESIDENT:  {C28}.  We might need this for the purpose
for today morning, right?
MR BURKE:  Yes.  It's a short errata sheet and it has
been signed.  But I'll take the witness to it and have
those confirmed as well, as part of his
evidence-in-chief.
PRESIDENT:  So let's bring the witness and let's put on
the screen the oath as well.  Let's see.
(Discussion off the record -- technical issues)
PRESIDENT:  Would you please put the oath on the screen?
MR BURKE:  The wording of the oath is in the protocol,
which is at {B1.15}, page 16, please.
I think the witness is waiting to be let in.
PRESIDENT:  Yes, please, the witness.
TECHNICIAN:  Sorry, sir, the witness is not yet here.  So
I can confirm that he's not yet joining.
MR BURKE:  So I'm just going to send a message to my
team.  Just calling him now, telling him to dial in.
(Pause).
He's just connecting now.  Sorry for the delay.
PRESIDENT:  No worries.
MR ALFREDO CRESPO BOTIA
WITNESS:  Good morning.
PRESIDENT:  Yes, good morning.  I don't see you on cam.
Can you turn on your camera, please?
MR BURKE:  If you scroll down, sir, I think he's right at
the bottom.
PRESIDENT:  Yes, I see now.
WITNESS:  You can see me now?
MR BURKE:  Alfredo?
WITNESS:  Yes.
PRESIDENT:  Yes.  Okay.
Would you like to start by swearing the oath or by
just affirmation?
WITNESS:  Well, I don't really know exactly the
difference.  Is there any --
PRESIDENT:  No, no, someone who have some belief, they
will swear by almighty God.  Otherwise they can just
affirm that they're going to say the truth and nothing
other.
WITNESS:  Okay, I'll go for the affirmation.  Yeah.
PRESIDENT:  Okay.  So if you please say "I", then your
full name, then read the second sentence on the
screen.
WITNESS:  Okay, I got it.
I, Alfredo Crespo, do solemnly, sincerely, and
truly declare and affirm to say all the truth and
nothing but the truth.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.
Can you please confirm whether any correction are
required to the content of your witness statement, or
there is no any correction?
WITNESS:  Yeah.  Well, there are, I think, three or four
corrections that have been submitted to the tribunal
according to my lawyer company.  Yeah.  There are
three or four, right, minor corrections.
MR BURKE:  Sir, I'll take the witness to those
corrections, that errata sheet as part of his
evidence-in-chief, if that's acceptable to the
tribunal.
PRESIDENT:  Yes.  Yes, please, go ahead.
MR BURKE:  Thank you.
Examination-in-chief by MR BURKE
MR BURKE:  Mr Crespo, good morning.
A. Good morning.
Q. Could you please -- you should have hard copies in
front of you, but for the screen -- for the
transcript, bundle reference {C1-1}.  You'll see and
you should have in front of you a document entitled
"Witness statement of Alfredo Crespo Botia".  That
document runs from {C1-1} to {C1-25}.  Do you see
that?
A. Yes, I can see.
Q. And can you confirm please, that that is your first
witness statement in this arbitration?
A. I confirm.
Q. And there is a signature in the middle of the page on
page {C1-25}.  Could you please confirm that is your
signature?
A. That is my signature.
Q. There are then three annexes to your first witness
statement.  The first one, annex 1, runs from {C2-1}
to {C2-27}.  Could you confirm, please, that is
annex 1 to your first witness statement in this
arbitration?
A. I confirm.
Q. There is then a second annex, annex 2, which is from
{C3-1} to {C3-3}.  Could you confirm that is the
second annex to your first witness statement in
arbitration?
A. That is the second annex, I confirm.
Q. And there is then a third annex which is C -- sorry,
that's an exhibit of your witness statement.  No,
there it is.  Yes, {C4-1} to {C4-4}, that is the third
annex to your witness statement in this arbitration;
correct?
A. Correct.  I confirm.
Q. And there is then a second witness statement.  That is
{C8-1}.  Again, you should have a hard copy of that.
That runs from {C8-1} through to {C8-17}.  Could you
confirm, please, that is your second witness statement
in this arbitration?
A. I confirm.
Q. There is a signature on page {C8-17}.  Could you
confirm, please, that is your signature?
A. That is my signature as well.
Q. And there is then a further witness statement at
{C14-1} that is titled third witness statement, and
that runs from {C14-1} to {C14-8}.
A. Yes.
Q. Could you confirm, please, that is your third witness
statement in this arbitration?
A. I confirm.
Q. There is a signature in the middle, or the bottom,
I should say, of {C14-8}.  Could you please confirm
that is your signature?
A. That is my signature.
Q. And could we please bring up {C28}, which is the
errata sheet.  And you'll see there is a document on
the screen in front of you.  You may not have it in
hard copy.  That runs from {C28-1} I think to {C28-3}.
If we just scroll just above that.
These are the corrections I understand you wish to
make to your first witness statement and to its
annexes.  Could you please confirm that these are the
corrections you wish to make as marked on this sheet?
A. I confirm.
Q. And there is a signature at the bottom of that page,
{C28-2}.  Could you please confirm that is your
signature?
A. That is my signature.
Q. And could you please confirm that the contents of your
three witness statements, as corrected by your
schedule of errata, are true to the best of your
information and belief?
A. This is true.
MR BURKE:  Thank you, Mr Crespo.  There will be some
questions.
A. Okay.
(Discussion off the record -- technical issues)
PRESIDENT:  Hello.  I don't know what happened, but for

I came back now.  I think I didn't miss anything.
You was checking your live transcript, Adrian?
MR BURKE:  We were, sir.  Yes.
PRESIDENT:  Yes, okay.  Are we ready now?
MR BURKE:  I believe so.  Mine is working.
PRESIDENT:  Yes, yes.  And are you okay now?
MR COLE:  Yes, I am.  Thank you.
PRESIDENT:  All right.  Perfect.
Yes, Mr Wygas, please go ahead.
MR WYGAS:  I'm grateful.
Cross-examination by MR WYGAS
MR WYGAS:  Mr Botia, can we just understand some basics,
first of all.  You say you were based on the
greenfield project site offices; yes?
A. Yes.  The office was based in the greenfield.
Q. And is that the office that Mr Atherton was also at?
A. Mr Paul Atherton?  Yes.
Q. Okay.  Can we then just look at what you give evidence
in relation to?  If we go to {C1}, your first witness
statement and paragraph 3.  We can see there the five
issues that that statement covers, yes?
A. Mm-hmm.
Q. And if we go to {C8}, that's your second witness
statement.  If we just go down to paragraph 5, we can
see again progress payments to Down Town; delays
caused by Danway; Down Town's various claims, yes?
A. Mm-hmm, yes.
Q. And then if we go to {C14} and paragraph 3 again, we
can see the three things that are covered in that.
A. I can see.
Q. Yeah.  So what your witness evidence relates to is it
relates to the performance of Down Town Construction
on the site, doesn't it, in relation to this project?
A. Yes.
Q. Now, Down Town Construction were on site for about
50 months, weren't they?
A. Yes.
Q. Now, you attended no site meetings with Down Town
Construction, did you?
A. No, I didn't.
Q. You didn't attend any meetings with managerial staff
from Down Town Construction, did you?
A. I did, in the context of the subcontract
administration.
Q. Now, Mr Cassese, is it Mr Cassese who was a site
operation director?
A. He was one of them during the course of the Down Town
execution of the works.  There were three different
ones, okay, site managers.  So, yes, Mr Cassese was
one of them.
Q. Yeah.  And he didn't normally attend weekly progress
meetings with Down Town, did he?
A. No, I don't think.  I think he attended those
meetings.  Those meetings were leaded by the
construction managers.
Q. Right.  Mr Savi, he's the operation director?
A. Correct.  At some point, yes.
Q. He did not attend the weekly progress meetings with
Down Town Construction, did he?
A. I'm not sure.  Maybe he attended some of them, but
definitely not all of them.  Yeah.
Q. Mr Di Mario, he's the TTSJV director.
A. Mm-hmm.
Q. Did you have any dealings with him?
A. Sorry, say again?
Q. Did you have any dealings with him?
A. Any?
Q. Dealings.  Did you speak to him?
A. To Mr Di Mario?  Yes, oftenly.
Q. Okay.  He rarely visited sites, didn't he?
A. I don't know how often he visited the site.  Trying to
be honest.
Q. Okay.  Who was Mr Coronella?
A. Coronella?  Mr Fabio Coronella?
Q. Yeah.
A. He was the planning manager for the brownfield area.
Q. Right.  Would he have a detailed knowledge of
Down Town Construction's progress on the site?
A. Well, he was the planning manager, so he managed all
the reporting, all the information regarding the
progress of all the subcontractors in the brownfield.
So he should have for Down Town as well.
Q. So Mr Coronella would understand what matters were
delaying Down Town Construction, wouldn't he?
A. Yes.
Q. Can we then look at paragraph 29 of your first witness
statement, please?  That's {C1-6}.  There we go.
So you say there, you talk about the process of
substitution.  And you say there:
"Whilst I was not involved directly in those
discussions, I knew about them from my own
discussions..."
And then you name Mr Cassese, Mr Savi, Mr Di Mario
and Mr Liberati; yes?
A. Yes.
Q. So it's Mr Cassese, Mr Savi, Mr Di Mario and
Mr Liberati.  Those are the ones who understood the
decisions in relation to substitution, yes --
A. Yes.
Q. -- about whether work can be substituted?
And you were told what the conclusion of those
decisions were, weren't you?
A. Yes.
Q. So if we wanted to understand the detail of why
substitution had been made or the reasons for those
decisions, we'd need to speak to one or more of
Mr Liberati, Mr Cassese, Mr Savi or Mr Di Mario,
wouldn't we?
A. Yes.
Q. Can we then go to paragraph 30 of your first witness
statement.  You then say:
"Mr Di Mario would then [take] a decision as to
what to do next."
Yeah?
A. Yeah, he was the project director, yeah.
Q. So you were not part of the decision-making process,
were you?
A. No, I wasn't.
Q. Okay.  Can we then look at the process of substitution
that you do give evidence on.  And if we go to
paragraph 30 of your first witness statement, which is
{C1-7}.  It's up on the screen.
You say five lines down, you're talking about the
issue of substitution:
"As part of this exercise, we would, between us,
produce an estimated comparison of the costs of
engaging different possible replacement
subcontractors..."
Yeah?
A. Correct.
Q. Now, that estimated comparison, that would be on the
basis of the volume of the work, of the relevant work,
in Down Town Construction's subcontract, wouldn't it?
A. Well, it would be an estimation of the quantities to
be performed for those works that were to be descoped,
to the best of our knowledge at that time, because
the --
Q. Would that be -- sorry, Mr --
A. No, sorry.
Q. I interrupted.  Carry on.
A. No, no, no.  I finished.
Q. Now, the works to be de -- I think substituted, to the
best of your knowledge, that would have to be the
works -- or would that have to be the works in
Down Town Construction's subcontract?
A. Yes.
Q. So the volume of the work then that you were going to
substitute would be the volume of the work that was in
Down Town Construction's subcontract?
A. Well, not necessarily the volume, because the
quantities in the subcontract are estimate as well.
So they may increase or decrease.
As I said, we took the part of the work that we
wanted to substitute, and analysed what the quantities
were.
Q. So are you saying that by the time of substitution,
the quantities that you were going to substitute of
a particular job would have moved on from what was in
the subcontract?
A. Moved on?  I don't know if I would say like this.
I would say the quantities, this part of the
quantities will be transferred to the substituted --
substitution subcontractor.
I don't know if I'm responding your question.
Q. Okay, well, Mr Botia, we can try again, don't worry.
When the decision was taken to substitute work
away from Down Town Construction, the volume of the
work, as I understand it from your evidence, would be
based on what you understood as at that time was
required by the project?
A. Yes.
Q. And that volume of work may be different to what was
in the subcontract, in Down's Town subcontract?
A. Yes.  May be different or not.
Q. That's all we need to understand, Mr Botia, at this
stage.
Now, can we then go to look at how the
substitution process works.  And can we go to {E3350},
please.
Now, do you recognise this form of document?
A. Yes.
Q. What is it?
A. This is a tabulation to try to find out possible other
subcontractors to substitute Down Town part of the
work, in this case for the unit 50.  Yeah.
Q. Okay.
Now, you talk about a substitution variation in --
we don't need to go to it -- in paragraph 39 of your
first witness statement.  I just want to understand
how this document works, the document on the screen
now works, in relation to a substitution variation.
Can we go to -- sorry, but before we do that,
let's just explain this document to make sure I
understand this.
The numbers in red, what are they?
Maybe we could just make the numbers slightly
bigger.
There we go.
What are the numbers in red there?
A. I guess we were re-marking.  I don't remember, but I
guess we were re-marking Down Town numbers.
Q. Right, well, it does say "Down Town" at the top.
Are you familiar with this document, Mr Botia?
A. If I am familiar with the tabulation?
Q. Yeah.
A. Yes, yes, this is called a BAR. It's a bid, a work
recommendation document that is done generally, just
to award a portion of the work in the project, for any
portion of the work in the project.  This is a
commercial tabulation including a technical
tabulation.  Yeah.
Q. So the first column with numbers in red, that's the
Down Town numbers, yes?
A. Correct.
Q. Then the column to the right of it is "CCT".  And that
is the cost for CCT to do the same work, so the
estimated cost, yes?
A. Correct.
Q. Right.  And then we have, to the right of that,
further subcontractors, yes?
A. Yes.
Q. Right.  Can we just talk about a substitution
variation, and you talk about a variation request to a
subcontractor.  I just want to understand how this
works, because let's take, for example, on the screen
at the moment, we have the figures from CCT, which
come out at about US$2.8 million, don't they?
A. Yes.
Q. I want to understand where that 2.8 comes from.
Can we look now at the substitution variation.  If
we go to {E946}.
Right, do you recognise this document?
A. Yes.
Q. This is a standard form document used on the project,
isn't it?
A. Yes.
Q. And this is the document which the subcontractor will
fill in, in relation to substituted -- or a request
for substituted works, yes?
A. Well, not only for substituted.  This is in general,
this is for as a variation to other subcontractor.  It
may be an additional work, it may be a modification
work or it may be a substitution for other
subcontractor's work.
Q. Okay.  Now, there are figures on this document.  Are
those figures inputted by the subcontractor?
A. The figures?
Q. Yeah, the actual cost.  So we can see, on this one we
can see US$9,000 odd, yes?
A. Yes.
Q. Who fills in that figure, the 9,000 odd?
Q. Yeah.
A. By subcontractor.  There are two different types of
request.  This is variation request by subcontractor.
Q. Yeah.
A. In this case it's subcontractor.  And there are
another variation which are variation requests by
contractor.  In this case, we fill in the request.
Yeah.
Q. So can we then go back to {E3350}.
Let's stick with CCT and the $2.9 million figure.
Yes?
A. Yes.
Q. Where did that $2.9 million figure come from?
A. From the quantities.  The key quantity we have on the
left.  Excavation 13,000 cubic, backfilling
10,000 cubic, and concrete works 2,289 cubic metres.
Yeah.
Q. And what rate did you use then to get to -- well,
let's just stick with the excavation at 13,000 cubic
metres.  You've come up with a figure of $974,000 odd;
what rate did you apply to that cubic metres, to the
13,000 cubic metres?
A. Well, I don't -- I mean, the details?  Okay, there
should be an attachment, I don't know, with the split
of the prices.  Okay?  There should be an attachment.
But in the case of excavation, I think it's very
straightforward.  We just need to divide 974,000 by
Now, I don't --
Q. Where did you get that rate from?
A. From CCT.
Q. Right.
A. CCT quotation, from the quotation.
Q. Right.  So CCT would give you the figures that you put
into this spreadsheet?
A. In the tabulation sheet, you mean?
Q. Yes.
A. Yes, yes.  Every subcontractor will provide a
quotation and we will use those quotations to fill in
the tabulation.
Q. Okay.  So now we're understanding the process you went
through in relation to substitution variations.
Can we now look at paragraph 38 of your first
witness statement which is at {C1-9}.  You there talk
about other subcontractors to which substitution
variations were issued.  CCT that we talked about a
moment ago.
A. Mm-hmm.
Q. MCSC and GMS?
A. Mm-hmm.
Q. Yeah?
A. Yes.
Q. Those were the main subcontractors that TTSJV went to
when substituting DTC's work, isn't it?
A. When substituting Down Town work?
Q. Yes.
A. Yes.
Q. Now, it's also right that CCT was the sister company
of GMS, isn't it?
A. Yeah, I think it's just stated in the tabulation, if
I don't recall.
Q. Yeah.
A. Okay.
Q. So in reality, if CCT and GMS are related companies,
let's just call them both GMS for now, Down Town's
work was really given to GMS and MCSC, wasn't it?
A. No, I don't agree.  They are different.  CCT and GEMS,
I don't -- I'm not sure, they don't belong to the same
group, do they?  I'm not sure now.
Q. Can we go to --
A. Maybe, or not.
Q. Just to clear that point up, can we go to paragraph 32
of this witness statement?
A. Okay.
Q. Do you remember reading this witness statement before
signing it?
A. Yes.
Q. Right.  Can you see the final sentence of the
paragraph 32:
"... CCT was a sister company to GEMS ..."
A. Yes, I was told that they were -- they belong to the
same owner, but I'm not sure if they belong to the
same group.  I mean, they have a different CR.  So for
us, it's different companies.  I was told that the
owner was the same.  Or -- no, let me recall
correctly.  The owner, the owner of GEMS is part of
the -- how to say that; I don't know how to say that,
sorry -- the council of CCT or the structure in CCT.
Q. Right.
A. So that's the sister relationship I was trying to
point out.  It's true that the owner of GEMS form part
of the board of CCT.
Q. Right.
A. I would say that.
Q. So what we know is that, as you said in your
evidence -- I don't think there's anything between
us -- that GEMS and CCT are related companies.  And
we'll just use that in the broadest terms, yes?
A. No, I wouldn't say that.
Q. Okay.  I'll leave that point there, because that's the
opposite of what your written witness evidence says.
Now, you were involved in issuing all the
substitution variations, weren't you?
A. Issuing, yes.
Q. Right.  So you saw them all?
A. Yes.
Q. Now, we'll come back to the variations in a moment,
but before we do, I'd just like to look at the form of
the subcontract.
Have you seen the allegation by Down Town that
TTSJV treated some subcontractors better than
Down Town?
A. I've been told the allegation by my counsel, yeah.
Q. Right.  And you have seen TTSJV's response, that it
treated Down Town the same as everyone else, yes?
A. I don't know if I've seen, but, yeah, I discussed with
my team about this point and we concluded that it is
not the case.
Q. Now, have you been told about Mr Ottaviani's evidence
yesterday?
A. No.
Q. Mr Ottaviani confirmed that the general terms and
conditions for subcontractors were all the same across
the project, yeah?
A. Yeah, they used to be, yeah.  Unless there is some --
unless there is some, let's say, comment from the
subcontractor, from the awardee.  If the awardee has
some comments, sometimes we change.  But in general,
they are more or less all the same.
Q. Exactly.
Now, we looked at excavation and the excavation
rates when we looked at the -- do you remember the
spreadsheet we looked at?  We looked at the excavation
rates.
A. Yeah.
Q. That's not specialised work, is it?
A. Excavation?  No, you can do by machine or by hand.
Q. Yeah.  And all the subcontractors that were doing
excavation had a re-measurable contract, didn't they?
A. Yes.
Q. So if they dug 10 per cent more, they would get paid
10 per cent more under their subcontracts, wouldn't
they?
A. I mean, in quantity?  If they do more in quantity?
Q. Yeah.
A. Yes, definitely.
Q. So when you were looking to substitute Down Town's
work, you would look to substitute that work to a
subcontractor who already did, in our example,
excavation, wouldn't you?
A. Well, in the case of CCT, they were new to the -- they
were not at the site at that time.
Q. Okay.  But they would give a rate.  They would then
have a subcontract with a rate for excavation,
wouldn't they?
A. Correct.
Q. And that rate would just be a -- and that subcontract
was a re-measurable contract?
A. Correct.
Q. So, can we just go and look at the general terms and
conditions.  If we go to {F1.4}.
Have you seen this document?
A. Yes.  I should have seen, because this is -- I cannot
see, but this is Down Town's or who, or CCT's?
Q. This is Down Town's but it's just --
A. Down Town's, okay.  I should have seen a review, yeah.
Q. Yeah.  Now, can we go to page 30.
This is in relation to variations, yes?
A. Yes.
Q. Can we go down to page 31 -- sorry, there.  Can you
see above 14.4, the final paragraph that says:
"For the purpose of this Article, and provided
that the quantities have been specified as
re-measurable, the adjustment to quantities
constitutes an adjustment of the Main Work but does
not constitute a Variation."
Do you see that?
A. Yes.
Q. So if, for example, excavation was added to another
subcontractor's contract, that would simply be an
increase in the quantities of their excavation,
wouldn't it?
A. Yes.
Q. So all they would be entitled to would be their rate
under the subcontract, multiplied by the amount of
excavation that they did?
A. Yes.
Q. Can we then look at early substitution, because you
deal with that -- or the earlier substitution, because
you deal with that in paragraphs 25 and 26 of your
first witness statement.  That's {C1-6}.
You can see paragraph 25, going into 26:
"Down Town --"
Sorry, this is your witness statement, yes?
A. Yes, yes.  Correct.
Q. "Down Town's performance issues began almost
immediately, as it failed properly to mobilise ..."
Do you see that?
A. Yes.
Q. As a result of Down Town's poor performance, it became
necessary for Down Town to assist -- I beg your
pardon, for TTSJV to assist Down Town with
producing -- with providing additional workers, yes?
A. Okay.
Q. Yeah.  So you're saying right from the start, you are
saying there are problems with Down Town?
A. Yes.  They were not mobilising quick enough, yes.
Q. You say those were problems which caused TTSJV to
reduce its work, yes?
A. But this is the early mobilisation, right.  This is
because we needed to award -- not award -- to
transfer, for instance, some tank foundations earlier,
even before Down Town could mobilise, to another
subcontractor.
Q. Which foundations did you need to deal with early on?
A. I don't -- this is in unit 51, D -- tank D, 1, 2, 3,
I think.  I'm not sure about the tacks of this, but
there were three big foundations for tanks that we
discovered to be FCC at the beginning.  And we made
it, because Down Town was not mobilised, we just had
another subcontractor to do it through a variation,
yes.
Q. Well, I think we'll come on to discuss that later
on --
A. Okay.
Q. -- Mr Botia, so we'll leave that there.  But we're
just talking about Down Town's alleged poor
performance at the start.
A. Okay.
Q. Can we then go to {E102}, please.
Do you recognise this document?
A. Oh, yeah.  This is Down Town contract, yeah,
subcontract.  Addendum 1, right?
Q. Yeah, and it's dated -- take it from me, it's dated
6th February 2020, so at the start of the works, isn't
it?
A. Yes.
Q. Can we go to page 3 of this document.  Can you see
there that the subcontract price has increased; from
US$43.5 million, it's increased by US$24.8 million.
Do you see that?
A. Yes.
Q. That's a substantial increase, isn't it?
A. It is.
Q. And that is a substantial increase that would not have
been given if it was thought that Down Town were not
